verdicts.rewritten_summary: GlobalGayz resident account ('Eddi', May 2009): documents how invisible gay life is — 'virtually nothing on the Internet about gay life in TCI'; notes ~2/3 of residents are not originally from the islands and full-citizen Belongers are a demographic minority versus foreigners, so there is no visible scene and privacy is the norm; useful as the on-the-ground social-climate read for a visitor.

UK HM Passport Office knowledge-base profile (Crown copyright 2025): official operational guidance covering nationality, legitimacy, adoption, gender recognition, civil partnerships and marriage, and documents for the territory — states adoption is legal and that 'transgender citizens are recognised in the Turks and Caicos Islands', i.e. the administering state's passport office handles gender-recognised documents for this jurisdiction.

TC Weekly News: Court of Appeal landmark ruling ordered the Director of Immigration to issue a residence permit to Timothy Haymon as the same-sex spouse of Richard Sankar — refusal on sexual-orientation grounds contravened constitutional guarantees; 'spouse' in the Immigration Ordinance read to include a same-sex spouse lawfully married in another jurisdiction, with equality/non-discrimination/private-life guarantees invoked (marriage definition left untouched). Directly relevant: same-sex partners of visitors/residents get residence recognition.

Klshepedia overview (published Apr 2026): same-sex sexual activity legal in the Turks and Caicos Islands since 2001 and discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is constitutionally banned — the two anchor legal facts for a visitor assessing exposure.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Chad: criminalisation section states the law criminalised consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults with punishments ranging from three months to two years' imprisonment — official current-law baseline for visitor exposure; report also covers societal abuses.

US State Dept 2010 Human Rights Report, Chad (pre-criminalisation baseline): law prohibited but did not define 'unnatural acts' with no evidence it was used against LGBT persons that year; no known LGBT organisations and few reports of violence, most persons discreet due to social strictures — documents the pre-2017 legal climate.

HuffPost/GroundTruth Project analysis: while further criminalisation attempts failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda, they succeeded in Chad and Nigeria — situates Chad's criminalisation drive within the broader wave of conservative anti-LGBT advocacy, relevant context for how the law's trajectory developed.

Human Dignity Trust country profile (fetched this session): Togo criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment plus a fine — the core exposure fact for a visitor.

AAEC Togo + Synergia alternative report to the UN Human Rights Committee (June 2021): the Togolese association works on HIV within MSM-TG populations under the National Strategic Plan 2016-2020, documents LGBT rights violations across Togo and francophone West Africa, and provides legal/judicial support to victims — evidence of an active civil-society documentation and assistance channel.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Togo: the law prohibits 'acts against nature committed with an individual of one's sex' (widely understood as same-sex conduct) and also the 'promotion of same-sex conduct', reaching advocacy and gender identity expression; the law was enforced, and violence/threats targeting LGBTTQI persons were listed among significant human-rights issues — official current-law + enforcement read.

Washington Blade (Aug 31, 2015): interviews with LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria (conducted 14-31 March 2015) include a Togo section — the author returned to Lomé, visited the site of a 2008 attack on him, and reports the capital's police are 'particularly merciless when dealing with LGBT locals and tourists', a rare on-the-ground note naming TOURIST exposure.

Thai Government PRD (05/08/2024): the Immigration Bureau launched 'Welcome Pride by Immigration' to mitigate concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports don't match their current appearance or gender — the entry-friction fix a trans visitor most needs to know about before arrival.

Outright International country overview (last updated Mar 12, 2026): Thailand became the first country in Southeast Asia to legalise same-sex marriage — bill passed its final Senate reading June 2024, in effect January 22, 2025, using gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms; its at-a-glance tables also carry the legal-status read.

Bangkok Post 'Pride in Action' forum (Lido Connect, 2025): advocates urge the government to expedite a gender-recognition law following marriage-equality, with public education framed as part of expanding rights protection — legal gender recognition is still pending post-SSM.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Nov 2025): when a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya in April, the community called it a hate crime but Thai law has no hate-crime designation — bias-motivated violence is handled as ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties or data collection; documents the accountability gap.

Globe (05/05/2025): following the Pattaya killing of a Thai trans woman by 42-year-old Chinese citizen Fu Tongyung after she refused his request for sex, LGBTQ+ groups urgently called for new hate-crime protections — names the perpetrator/victim facts and the resulting legal-protection push.

HRW report 'People Can't Be Fit into Boxes' (Dec 2021): no route for transgender people to obtain legal documentation reflecting their gender identity; even affirmative measures like first-name change leave discretionary power with officials; anti-discrimination protections are not fully enforced — the documentation gap a trans visitor may also feel.

NZZ in English (May 2025): the conservative government introduced progressive trans laws including free hormone treatments with little public opposition; trans people report greater societal acceptance and higher company positions than typical in the West — explains why social climate outruns the legal framework.

LegalClarity (June 2026): marriage equality since January 2025 and anti-discrimination law since 2015, yet no mechanism to change the sex marker on birth certificate, national ID or passport (title prefixes locked to sex at birth; Name Act 1962 partial workaround) — precise current documentation-status read.

Fulcrum/ISEAS (June 2025): analyses the government's push to position Thailand as an LGBTQ+ tourism hub (Bangkok Pride 4 June backdrop) alongside marriage equality — weighs opportunities and challenges of a state strategy whose motives range from genuine commitment to economic opportunism; relevant to how welcoming institutions are pitched to visitors.

G.A.M. Legal Alliance (Thai firm) analysis of the post-same-sex-marriage landscape: marriage equality closes practical gaps for couples — exclusion from property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims — the concrete before/after of the January 2025 change.

GlobalGayz archive (2007-10): index of Thai LGBT news of the era — the National Human Rights Commission's role, constitutional-charter gay-rights campaigns, Phuket acceptance/rejection accounts, and the 'Please call me Miss' debate on trans legal title — historical baseline showing how long recognition questions have been live.

IPHR report 'Rights for All?' (Feb 2024): consensual same-sex relations decriminalised since 1998, yet authorities introduced a police register of LGBTIQ people in 2016; 2022/2023 police raids brought forced HIV-testing and arbitrary criminal charges; ill-treatment, sexual abuse and extortion by police documented; the 2022 anti-discrimination law fails to address discrimination — the systematic-risk evidence for a visitor.

Outright International overview (updated Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal throughout the country since independence, no SOGI non-discrimination protection; in 2024 ECOM recorded 27 human-rights violation cases against LGBT people with police arbitrary arrests, blackmail and extortion; a 2017 government registry of 'proven' LGBT persons flagged — legality without safety.

ECOM study (2024) on trans people's access to medical services incl. HIV prevention/treatment and HRT across the EECA region, with a Tajikistan country coordinator contributing — maps what gender-affirming/HIV care is actually reachable in-country and includes guidance for trans migrants.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): police lure LGBT people into fake meetings to register them in a database, harvest social-media contacts and extort money (10+ cases in Sughd); forced/sham marriages used against LGBT people with police inaction; the 2022 anti-discrimination law only partially aligns with UN standards — quantified police-entrapment risk.

ECOM legislative analysis (2020): comparative analysis identifying legal barriers and gaps for gay men, MSM and trans people in Tajikistan, built from a questionnaire completed by local partners — documents where the written law protects but practice does not.

HRW World Report 2017, Tajikistan chapter: the human-rights situation deteriorated sharply in 2016 — opposition leadership sentenced, human-rights lawyers imprisoned, and a predetermined referendum extending presidential rule — the repressive state context surrounding LGBT life.

Global Voices (Jan 20, 2013): despite decriminalisation 15 years earlier (1998) there is very little tolerance; those who disclose orientation become targets of physical and psychological abuse including from police, and the community remains one of the most closed in society — social-climate evidence predating the 2016 registry.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the April 2022 Criminal Code not only kept the 'sodomy' provisions but increased both the severity and scope of punishments; torture and inhumane treatment remain present throughout the country with relatives reporting LGBTI people subjected to them — the current penal-risk read.

US State Dept 2021 Human Rights Report, Turkmenistan: lists among significant human-rights issues the existence of laws criminalizing consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults, alongside officials in security services committing abuses and engaging in corruption with impunity — official assessment of law plus enforcement climate.

EHPV mid-term UPR stakeholder submission (2020): LGBT persons and people living with HIV in Turkmenistan 'have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights'; identifies article 135 of the Criminal Code criminalising consensual same-sex acts between adult men as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination, and notes increasing flight abroad.

ECOM legislative analysis, 'Legislative analysis related to LGBT rights and HIV in Turkmenistan' (Tallinn, 2019, 11pp, with Turkmen.news): maps the legal landscape and barriers for LGBT people and PLHIV — deliberately compiled so NGOs, community activists and government can use it when planning advocacy; the standing legal-baseline reference for the country.

Columbia Law School (May 1, 2007): the Sexuality and Gender Law Clinic secured US asylum (DHS) for an anonymous Turkmen woman persecuted because she is a lesbian and for her political opinions — believed to be the first-ever asylum granted to a lesbian from Turkmenistan; documents persecution grounds cited by people fleeing the country.

Australian Volunteers Program Pride Guide, Timor-Leste: country snapshot for volunteers — same-sex sexual acts decriminalised in 1975; the UN Human Rights Council joint statement on SOGI was adopted in 2011; Timor-Leste voted in favour of the 2013 UN resolution on vulnerability/disability... sets out the legal and policy context for living openly as a volunteer.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: New Naratif (June 2018): Timor-Leste's first-ever Pride parade in 2017 drew international attention and a televised endorsement from the Prime Minister, while the report also captures day-to-day rejection (the organiser's family messages) — social-climate depth beyond the headline acceptance.

VOA (July 2018): East Timor held its second annual LGBT pride parade in Dili on July 20, cementing a regional leadership role while neighbours Indonesia and Malaysia turn hostile — the open-environment evidence for visitors.

Star Observer (July 2019): an estimated 3,000 people joined the 'Marsa Diversidade' Pride March in Dili on July 12 — six times the turnout of the 2017 first parade; President Francisco Guterres publicly backed the event ('I am a President for all people'). Quantified growth of visible acceptance.

Outright International overview (updated Mar 2026): the Criminal Offences Act outlaws same-sex activity between men and women with a maximum of 10 years' imprisonment (no evidence of enforcement in recent years), AND criminalises any male soliciting in public 'for an immoral purpose' with intent to deceive as to his true sex — a direct trans-expression statute on the books; no gender recognition.

Washington Blade (Feb 2018): Cyclone Gita 'tore off' part of the roof of Tonga's LGBTI drop-in center and shelter on Tongatapu (Nuku'alofa) with winds over 120 mph, damaging bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI Tongans — documents the fragility of the country's only community shelter infrastructure.
